name: Atlas Grill
summary: Stress-test an idea through pointed questions.
intro: Find unclear decisions and weak assumptions before they become implementation work.
use: Grilling is the default. Request With Docs explicitly when answers should also become documentation.

modes.title: Grilling
modes.description: Challenge the plan through focused questions.
modes.example: Use atlas-grill to challenge this plan for replacing our billing provider. Ask one question at a time.

modes.title: With Docs
modes.description: Grill the plan and maintain its documentation when explicitly requested.
modes.example: Use atlas-grill with docs to work through our permissions model and record the decisions.

note: With Docs is never selected automatically.
origin: Combines Matt Pocock’s Grilling and Grill with Docs, with shared Domain Modeling references.

name: Atlas Wayfinder
summary: Map a large effort into decisions and resolve the next useful one.
intro: Keep a large effort navigable across sessions through linked decision tickets.
use: Invoke explicitly for work too large for one session, using the configured tracker or bundled local fallback.

modes.title: Map
modes.description: Chart the destination, decisions, blockers and available next work.
modes.example: Use atlas-wayfinder to map the unresolved decisions in our multi-session billing migration.

modes.title: Resolve
modes.description: Work through the next decision and update the map.
modes.example: Use atlas-wayfinder to resume the billing map and resolve the next unblocked decision.

note: Research and Prototype remain independent skills for their ticket types; Atlas Setup checks those dependencies.
origin: Adapts Matt Pocock’s Wayfinder with bundled Grilling, Domain Modeling and a local tracker fallback.

name: Atlas To Spec
summary: Turn a settled conversation into an actionable specification.
intro: Capture what has already been decided, connect it to the codebase, and leave a specification someone can implement.
use: Use after a conversation has enough context to define the work. Atlas synthesizes the existing decisions instead of starting another interview.

modes.title: Specification
modes.description: Synthesize the agreed behavior, implementation decisions and test seams into an actionable specification.
modes.example: Use atlas-to-spec to turn our agreed checkout changes into a local specification.

note: Tracker publication follows your project context and authorization.
origin: Adapted from Matt Pocock’s To Spec, with Atlas’s approach to local specifications and tracker publication.

name: Atlas To Tickets
summary: Break a specification into useful, connected slices.
intro: Turn a plan, spec, or conversation into tracer-bullet tickets with explicit dependencies.
use: Use when the direction is clear and the next step is making the work executable. Each ticket should deliver an observable slice of behavior.

modes.title: Tickets
modes.description: Create tracer-bullet vertical slices with explicit blocking relationships and save them to the agreed destination.
modes.example: Use atlas-to-tickets to split this checkout spec into vertical slices with blocking dependencies. Save them locally.

note: Each ticket should describe a deliverable slice and the work that blocks it.
origin: Adapted from Matt Pocock’s To Tickets, with Atlas’s local ticket templates and publication workflow.

name: Atlas Implement
summary: Design first, test first, or implement from official documentation.
intro: Choose the implementation method the task needs, or combine complementary methods.
use: Use Architect for design decisions, TDD for test-first behavior, and Source-Driven for version-sensitive framework or API work.

modes.title: Architect
modes.description: Compare designs before choosing interfaces, types and module ownership.
modes.example: Use atlas-implement with Architect to compare ways to model multiple deposition records before changing the API.

modes.title: TDD
modes.description: Prove behavior with a failing test, implementation and refactoring.
modes.example: Use atlas-implement with TDD to fix the pager skipping the last result. Start with a failing behavior test.

modes.title: Source-Driven
modes.description: Ground version-sensitive implementation in official documentation.
modes.example: Use atlas-implement with Source-Driven to implement uploads using the official docs for our installed SDK version.

note: Routine implementation does not require Architect. Combine methods when their needs apply.
origin: Combines Matt Pocock’s TDD, Addy Osmani’s Source-Driven Development and Pstack’s Architect with bundled supporting methods.

name: Atlas Verify
summary: Verify behavior with evidence or maintain reusable project checks.
intro: Run QA, build a reusable verifier, keep it current, or assess a performance claim.
use: Use Run to verify implemented behavior; choose Create or Maintain only when the requested result is reusable verification assets.

modes.title: Run · Feature
modes.description: Verify implemented behavior against the change and conversation, with recorded evidence and a structured report.
modes.example: Use atlas-verify in Run mode to verify the completed drawer in my logged-in browser session and produce a report.

modes.title: Run · QA list
modes.description: Run an existing QA list in full or select checks affected by a named change. Report checks that did not run.
modes.example: Use atlas-verify in Run mode to run the full project QA list before release and report every result.

modes.title: Create
modes.description: Build a reusable project verifier and feature map.
modes.example: Use atlas-verify in Create mode to build a reusable project verifier for the deposition drawer and its feature map.

modes.title: Maintain
modes.description: Audit and update an existing project verifier.
modes.example: Use atlas-verify in Maintain mode to update our existing drawer verifier for multiple deposition records.

modes.title: Performance
modes.description: Measure or assess a speedup, regression or benchmark claim.
modes.example: Use atlas-verify in Performance mode to test whether the new updates query is faster than the baseline under equivalent conditions.

note: Verification does not authorize product repairs. Reports and measurements disclose skipped checks and evidence gaps.
origin: Combines Product Engineering’s PE Verify report engine with Pstack’s verifier lifecycle and benchmark methods.

name: Atlas Review
summary: Review code, interface changes and motion with evidence.
intro: Review code, judge static checks, or assess interface motion with a method matched to the question.
use: Use when you need findings and evidence before deciding what to change. Reviewing a change does not, by itself, authorize fixes.

modes.title: Code
modes.description: Assess repository standards and originating requirements, keeping the Standards and Spec reports distinct.
modes.example: Use atlas-review in Code mode to review this branch against the checkout spec and repository standards.

modes.title: Adversarial
modes.description: Challenge changes with independent reviewers and reconcile their findings.
modes.example: Use atlas-review in Adversarial mode to challenge our assumption that the new permission checks prevent cross-firm access.

modes.title: Impact
modes.description: Trace what could break beyond the diff and check the relevant evidence.
modes.example: Use atlas-review in Impact mode to trace which consumers could break when we change record-list serialization.

modes.title: Static
modes.description: Run scoped lint and type checks, then judge the findings.
modes.example: Use atlas-review in Static mode to run lint and typechecks for the changed packages and assess the findings.

modes.title: Motion
modes.description: Review animation against specialist standards.
modes.example: Use atlas-review in Motion mode to assess this drawer transition for interruption, timing and reduced motion.

modes.title: Interface Changes
modes.description: Assess interface problems introduced or worsened by a diff, separating them from pre-existing findings.
modes.example: Use atlas-review in Interface mode to review this branch’s drawer changes on desktop and mobile. Separate new problems from existing ones.

modes.title: Interface Audit
modes.description: Assess an existing screen or flow for usability, accessibility, hierarchy and copy.
modes.example: Use atlas-review in Interface mode to audit the existing updates page for hierarchy, accessibility and confusing interactions.

modes.title: Motion Audit
modes.description: Survey existing motion and prepare prioritized improvement plans.
modes.example: Use atlas-review in Motion Audit mode to survey onboarding animations and prepare a prioritized improvement plan.

note: Review does not authorize product fixes. Atlas Verify supplies behavior checks when requested or needed.
origin: Combines Matt Pocock’s code review, Jakub Krehel’s interface review and Emil Kowalski’s motion methods. Static review and integration rulings are authored by Atlas. Pstack supplies Adversarial and Impact methods.

name: Atlas Explain
summary: Explain how code works, why it exists, or teach it through conversation.
intro: Build a useful understanding of a codebase while keeping evidence and uncertainty visible.
use: Choose How, Why or Teach. Without a mode, the agent asks before investigating.

modes.title: How
modes.description: Trace architecture, runtime flow and ownership.
modes.example: Use atlas-explain in How mode to trace what happens between clicking Save and the database write.

modes.title: Why
modes.description: Investigate decisions and constraints through historical evidence.
modes.example: Use atlas-explain in Why mode to investigate why this service uses polling instead of subscriptions.

modes.title: Teach
modes.description: Build understanding at your pace through conversation.
modes.example: Use atlas-explain in Teach mode to help me understand this state machine. Check my understanding as we go.

note: Explanation keeps code and external records read-only. Matt Pocock’s learning-workspace Teach remains independent.
origin: Combines Pstack’s How, Why and conversational Teach with shared Unslop guidance.

name: HTML UI
summary: Make an interface idea concrete before committing to it.
intro: Explore a product interface as an HTML wireframe or a polished, interactive model.
use: Use when a layout, interaction, or product flow is easier to judge by seeing it. Choose the fidelity that answers the question.

modes.title: Wireframe
modes.description: Test hierarchy, layout, and task structure without committing to visual polish.
modes.example: Use html-ui in Wireframe mode to explore the hierarchy and navigation of this settings flow.

modes.title: Model
modes.description: Show a polished mockup or working product flow, preserving the agreed content and structure.
modes.example: Use html-ui in Model mode to turn our agreed checkout wireframe into a polished interactive model.

note: Choose a mode explicitly when fidelity matters. Model work uses the independently available Design Artifact guidance.
origin: Combines the Wireframe and Prototype methods from Plannotator’s Effective HTML, with small adaptations for Atlas’s skill setup.

name: Atlas Craft
summary: Refine the visual details, accessibility and copy of a real interface.
intro: Improve the details of a production interface while keeping its accepted identity and foundations.
use: Use when the direction is established and the interface needs better execution. Select one method or combine complementary methods.

modes.title: Color
modes.description: Refine palettes and tokens, check rendered contrast, and improve color usage.
modes.example: Use atlas-craft in Color mode to improve this form’s contrast while preserving the brand palette.

modes.title: Type
modes.description: Work on font choice, sizing, wrapping, and typographic detail.
modes.example: Use atlas-craft in Type mode to fix the heading hierarchy and awkward wrapping on this page.

modes.title: Layout
modes.description: Improve spacing, alignment, grouping, responsive behavior, and spatial RTL.
modes.example: Use atlas-craft in Layout mode to improve the mobile drawer’s spacing and grouping.

modes.title: Accessibility
modes.description: Improve semantics, keyboard paths, focus, forms and assistive-technology behavior.
modes.example: Use atlas-craft in Accessibility mode to fix the dialog’s keyboard flow, focus handling and field labels.

modes.title: UI Polish
modes.description: Refine surfaces, elevation, icons and optical alignment.
modes.example: Use atlas-craft in UI Polish mode to refine this toolbar’s icons, surfaces and optical alignment.

modes.title: Copy
modes.description: Improve labels, errors, empty states, confirmations and localized strings.
modes.example: Use atlas-craft in Copy mode to clarify these validation errors and the empty-state action.

note: New visual direction belongs to design work. Craft preserves the project’s accepted identity.
origin: Combines six Jakub Krehel interface methods with direct links between bundled methods and shared motion guidance from Emil Kowalski.

name: Atlas Motion
summary: Build interface motion or identify worthwhile animation opportunities.
intro: Construct interface animations and physical interactions with methods suited to the behavior.
use: Use for a transition, animated interface, or a direct manipulation gesture. Animate and Fluid can work together when they serve different parts of the task.

modes.title: Animate
modes.description: Construct an interface animation or transition.
modes.example: Use atlas-motion in Animate mode to build a drawer transition that preserves our existing motion tokens.

modes.title: Fluid
modes.description: Handle direct manipulation, momentum, and interruptible springs.
modes.example: Use atlas-motion in Fluid mode to make this draggable sheet respond naturally to release velocity and interruption.

modes.title: Opportunities
modes.description: Propose motion where it helps, reject unnecessary animation, and leave product code unchanged.
modes.example: Use atlas-motion in Opportunities mode to identify where motion would clarify onboarding. Leave product code unchanged.

note: Opportunities is read-only. Animate and Fluid build within the authorized scope; React Native and Expo are outside this package.
origin: Combines Emil Kowalski’s Animate, Apple Design and Find Animation Opportunities, with Atlas handoffs and motion ownership.

name: Animated-Driven Frontend
summary: Engineer the runtime behind demanding motion.
intro: Apply frontend engineering knowledge to synchronized scroll sequences, progress gestures, WebGL effects, and rendering performance.
use: Invoke this skill explicitly when motion depends on runtime architecture, shared progress, asset loading, or GPU work.

modes.title: Interaction systems
modes.description: Coordinate shared progress, seeking, holds, drawing, and synchronized feedback.
modes.example: Use animated-driven-frontend to coordinate this scroll sequence, progress indicator and seek control around one progress value.

modes.title: Rendering pipeline
modes.description: Handle WebGL assets, GPU uploads, effects, adaptive quality, and mobile rendering.
modes.example: Use animated-driven-frontend to investigate first-use stalls in this WebGL scene and plan asset loading for mobile devices.

modes.title: Frontend constraints
modes.description: Manage ownership, dependencies, loading, failures, and accessible motion.
modes.example: Use animated-driven-frontend to assess this animation’s resource cleanup, loading failures and reduced-motion fallback.

note: Test uncertain effects with a bounded sample before expanding them. Keep one authoritative state for synchronized systems.

name: Atlas Mode
summary: Work across Atlas skills and inner methods in one mode.
intro: Enter Atlas Mode once to apply clearly selected methods and get help choosing between materially different workflows.
use: Describe your task in your own words. Clear intent selects a method directly; consequential alternatives are explained with a recommendation before you choose. The mode carries the selected approach through follow-ups, including manual packages such as Wayfinder and Retro.

modes.title: Clear task
modes.description: Apply a method already selected by the request and continue the agreed work.
modes.example: Use atlas-mode to implement this feature test-first, then verify the completed behavior.

modes.title: Choose an approach
modes.description: Explain materially different workflows and inner methods, recommend one, and wait for your choice.
modes.example: Use atlas-mode to help me choose how to plan this migration. Explain the relevant skills and inner methods before starting.

note: Advice stays advisory until you select an approach. Tracking, Audit Trail and other opt-ins retain their conditions. Atlas Setup remains separately requested. Missing skills are reported.
origin: An Atlas-authored working mode over its independently usable skills.

name: Writing for Humans
summary: Make substantial prose worth the reader’s effort.
intro: Write, revise, or critique documentation, articles, explainers, and other substantial prose without flattening the author’s meaning or voice.
use: Invoke this skill for human-facing writing. Match the genre, intended meaning, audience, and permitted degree of revision before changing the words.

modes.title: Create
modes.description: Build prose around a clear promise and the reader’s context.
modes.example: Use writing-for-humans to write an introduction to this API for developers making their first request.

modes.title: Revise
modes.description: Make the material clearer while preserving the author’s stance and voice.
modes.example: Use writing-for-humans to revise this guide for clarity while preserving my voice and factual qualifications.

modes.title: Critique
modes.description: Assess the draft’s meaning, structure, evidence, and reader effort.
modes.example: Use writing-for-humans to critique this article’s argument and reader flow without rewriting it.

modes.title: Technical Writing
modes.description: Write usable technical documentation with accurate commands, explicit prerequisites and clear structure.
modes.example: Use writing-for-humans to turn these setup notes into a technical how-to with checked commands and prerequisites.

modes.title: Articles and newsletters
modes.description: Shape arguments, openings and reader progression while preserving the author’s voice.
modes.example: Use writing-for-humans to improve this newsletter’s opening and progression while keeping its conversational voice.

modes.title: Visual explanations
modes.description: Use a visual when it materially reduces the effort of understanding a mechanism or relationship.
modes.example: Use writing-for-humans to explain this retry flow with a visual that makes the failure paths easier to understand.

modes.title: Unslop
modes.description: Remove generic AI writing patterns while preserving facts, uncertainty and voice.
modes.example: Use writing-for-humans to remove generic AI phrasing from this draft while preserving its meaning and voice.

note: Agent-facing instructions belong to the independent Writing for Agents skill. This package includes shared Unslop guidance and a conditional technical-documentation method.
origin: Includes Pstack’s Unslop and Technical Writing, with adaptations that preserve author voice, factual qualifications, and repository conventions.

name: Team Up
intro: Select subagent roles, models, and reasoning effort when delegation or isolated context materially helps.
use: Use when the work benefits from a team. Choose the smallest capable team and match each assignment to an available role.

modes.title: Delegation
modes.description: Choose useful work, roles, models and reasoning effort.
modes.example: Use team-up’s Delegation mode to have one agent inspect the API contract while another implements the component.

modes.title: Arena
modes.description: Compare independent candidates and synthesize the strongest design.
modes.example: Use team-up in Arena mode to compare two complete designs for record-list persistence, select a base and combine useful strengths.

modes.title: Swarm
modes.description: Coordinate partitioned work, competing solutions or a combination.
modes.example: Use team-up in Swarm mode to investigate missing saved records across persistence, serialization and UI state, then consolidate the evidence.

note: Delegation is the lighter option for ordinary assignments. Swarm adds explicit coverage or race rules and one consolidated report. Arena compares complete candidates and synthesizes a result.
origin: Combines Atlas’s role and model selection policy with Pstack’s Arena and Swarm methods.

name: Tracking Implementation
summary: Keep the state of a build easy to resume.
intro: Maintain a durable implementation record alongside the chosen executor, with progress, validation, and review evidence.
use: Use when you explicitly ask to track work or resume an existing implementation record. A request to implement alone does not activate tracking.

modes.title: Start
modes.description: Create the smallest useful implementation record from the supplied work context.
modes.example: Use tracking-implementation to track this feature in a local HTML record alongside the executor.

modes.title: Maintain
modes.description: Keep execution state and evidence current alongside the executor.
modes.example: Use tracking-implementation to update the active record with this implementation slice, its blockers and validation evidence.

modes.title: Resume
modes.description: Read the existing record and source material before continuing.
modes.example: Use tracking-implementation to resume the implementation from this record and recover the pending work.

modes.title: Audit Trail
modes.description: On request, keep an append-only decision log and reconcile it against run evidence.
modes.example: Use tracking-implementation with Audit Trail for this migration. Keep decision evidence alongside the implementation record.

note: The checkpoint gate runs Code plus applicable Interface Changes, Motion, Impact or Adversarial reviews, each with a concrete question. The executor performs the work; Tracking records state. Audit Trail is optional. Verification remains independently selected, and coverage gaps stay explicit.
origin: Uses HumanLayer’s Show Me for presentation and Pstack’s Show Me Your Work for optional decision audits. Atlas supplies the tracking state, evidence requirements, and review workflow.

name: Atlas Retro
summary: Diagnose session friction or prevent recurring mistakes.
intro: Review how an agent worked, then choose whether to propose improvements or implement prevention.
use: Invoke Atlas Retro for a session retrospective. Diagnose is the default; request Enforce explicitly to implement prevention within the selected scope.

modes.title: Diagnose
modes.description: Inspect the selected session and propose environment improvements, ordered by severity.
modes.example: Use atlas-retro in Diagnose mode to inspect why this session repeatedly lost the agreed scope. Propose improvements.

modes.title: Enforce
modes.description: Implement authorized recurring-mistake prevention and prove it catches a real past failure.
modes.example: Use atlas-retro in Enforce mode to prevent the recurring date-format mistake with an automated check and prove it catches the past failure.

note: An ordinary correction does not trigger repository edits. Evidence gaps and unobserved CI runs remain explicit.
origin: Combines Matt Pocock’s Retro with Pstack’s Correct, with an explicit boundary between advice and implementation.

name: Atlas Setup
summary: Check dependencies, stack alignment and obsolete installations.
intro: Compare installed skills with the current Atlas stack and the dependencies of the packages you use.
use: Invoke to find missing dependencies or recommended stack additions and review installations that may be obsolete.

modes.title: Inspect
modes.description: Compare source-aware inventory with the current stack and dependency registry.
modes.example: Use atlas-setup to compare my installed skills with the current Atlas stack and report missing dependencies.

modes.title: Add
modes.description: Offer missing skills and install only the selections you authorize.
modes.example: Use atlas-setup to offer missing skills with their sources and install commands. Let me choose which to install.

modes.title: Cleanup
modes.description: Show exact obsolete-installation candidates and remove only explicitly approved targets.
modes.example: Use atlas-setup to propose obsolete installations for cleanup, with exact paths and scope. Wait for my approval before removing them.

note: Skills outside the stack may be intentional. Removal requires approval of the named targets and scope; unavailable current manifests are disclosed.
